name: Judge
label: Revelation
lede: A drummer who was tired of preaching peace wrote the angriest straight edge songs in New York, recorded the album twice, and then spent twenty years away from the monster he'd built.

eras.title: Lyrics from a Florida junkyard
eras.text: Mike Ferraro was drumming for Youth of Today and chafing at its non-violent message. He wrote his own songs on the road, quit, named the new band a week later, and asked Porcell to help him make it the most militant straight edge band anyone could imagine.

years.h: The drummer quits to say it his way
years.p: Parked in a Florida junkyard on a Youth of Today tour, Ferraro fills a notebook with lyrics. Back in New York he tells [[Ray Cappo|e8357f9d-f7f5-4858-a766-aef004bb38a6]] he's leaving, and comes up with the name Judge a week later.

years.h: A Brooklyn apartment, a two-man band
years.p: Ferraro is living with Porcell, Al Brown and Cappo. Porcell pushes him to turn the songs into a real band, and signs on to play guitar and bass.

q: I was doing everything to get that reaction.
years.src: Vice: Behind the Quiet, Part II · Wikipedia
years.h: New York Crew 7" · Schism Records
years.p: Porcell on guitar and bass, Ferraro singing and drumming. Five songs, including a cover of Blitz's Warriors, out on the label Porcell ran with Alex Brown.
years.xp:
Porcell balked at some of the first lyrics, telling Ferraro he was copping to crimes, and Ferraro rewrote an ending. What stayed in still started trouble: a line about Boston was taken as a direct challenge by the Boston crew around Choke.

Ferraro says he was chasing exactly that reaction, and was still shocked when it came.

years.h: First show: the Anthrax, with borrowed hands
years.p: To play live, Ferraro and Porcell bring in [[Drew Thomas|ebc66701-0d59-49c9-ae21-4937edb96a6a]] from [[Bold|b024b1bd-2020-4b7c-83f7-4660133c89fa]] and Jimmy Yu on bass. Yu and [[Luke Abbey|6ab9b327-0f98-4515-907c-13078f426cc5]] become the 1988–89 rhythm section.

eras.title: So good they recorded it twice
eras.text: Judge's first album cost real money at Chung King in Manhattan, and the band hated it. They started over in Rhode Island, and Revelation quietly pressed the rejected version for the fans who'd already paid.

years.h: Into Chung King with a new rhythm section
years.p: [[Sammy Siegler|869c662b-574c-46ac-acf6-3dc6f025fd5a]] on drums and Matt Pincus on bass. The session runs up a real bill, and the band rejects the results.

years.big: 110 copies of the album they threw away
years.src: Revelation Records pressing history · Wikipedia: Bringin' It Down
years.h: Chung King Can Suck It
years.p: To cover preorders while the band re-records, Revelation presses the rejected Chung King session on white vinyl and ships it to the kids who'd already paid. Two of its songs never made the final album.
years.xp:
The plan was 100. The plant made 110, and the extra ten had the first zero in the hand-numbered /100 written over with a 1. Both Jordan Cooper and Porcell believed only three test pressings existed; Porcell sold one thinking it was a Bringin' It Down test.

Copies now sell for over a thousand dollars, and according to Wikipedia one went for as much as $6,600 on eBay. Revelation has said it never made money on them.

years.h: Bringin' It Down · Revelation REV 15
years.p: Re-recorded at Normandy Sound in Rhode Island, the room where the [[Cro-Mags|9ffa627f-32c2-4cb1-bfad-00cf348abc70]] made Best Wishes, and produced by Porcell and Tom Soares. Nine songs in 22 minutes, metal riffing on a hardcore frame. The label's own tag line: so good they had to record it twice.

years.h: Rev reissues New York Crew as REV 14
years.p: 4,000 on black vinyl and 1,000 on blue, in an orange sleeve.

eras.title: The kids took it literally
eras.text: Judge had set out to provoke, and the provocation worked too well. The last records got darker and more reflective, while the shows filled with fights and worse, and Ferraro decided he couldn't stop what he'd started.

years.h: There Will Be Quiet... 7" · Revelation REV 20
years.p: [[Lars Weiss|c60d8790-7786-4df8-8647-7f8b2ca02c17]] joins on guitar. The Storm and Forget This Time show a slower, bleaker Judge; the CD adds a cover of Led Zeppelin's When the Levee Breaks.

years.h: The old bass player becomes a monk
years.p: Jimmy Yu, Judge's bassist in 1988–89, is ordained a Chan Buddhist monk under Master Sheng Yen, taking the name Guogu. He goes on to a Princeton PhD in 2008 and a job teaching religion at Florida State University.

q: Every word I ever wrote was thrown back into my face.
years.h: The last tour, and a walk away
years.p: On the last tour the violence stops being theater. At a show in Ybor City, Tampa, the Village Voice reported, racial slurs and white power chants start early in the set and a group attacks a Black man in the crowd. Ferraro confronts it from the stage. Judge ends that year.
years.xp:
From the stage Ferraro asked what six guys on one older man proved, and asked the room to get through the last song in peace. It was a pattern, not one night: at another stop someone called the house the band was staying in and asked Ferraro to go beat up members of the KKK holding a rally in town.

Maximum Rock'N'Roll had long criticized the band's militant edge, and Ferraro later admitted provocation was the point. He told the Voice he felt responsible, big-time, that kids were fighting while singing his lyrics at him, and that he couldn't stop what he'd put in motion. So he left.

eras.title: Ferraro goes quiet, the records don't
eras.text: The singer left the scene almost completely. The band's recordings kept circulating, officially and otherwise, until Revelation gathered everything onto one disc.

years.h: The Chung King tapes get out
years.p: Bootlegs, not Revelation releases: No Apologies: The Chung King Sessions and Revelation Can Suck It put the rejected session back in circulation, alongside a live WNYU broadcast, Vivo En WNYU.

years.h: Mike Judge and Old Smoke
years.p: Ferraro's Neil Young-leaning acoustic project with former Judge roadie Todd Schwartz releases the Sights 12" on Revelation. Then he mostly disappears from music.

years.h: What We Said... And Where It Went
years.p: A first retrospective while the band stays dormant.

years.h: What It Meant: The Complete Discography
years.p: Everything in one place, sixteen years after Bringin' It Down.

eras.title: Twenty years, then Webster Hall
eras.text: A radio appearance drew Ferraro back out after roughly two decades away. The reunion that followed was two nights in New York, then the world, and a documentary that told the story in the band's own words.

years.h: Back on the air
years.p: Ferraro turns up on Black N' Blue Takeover on East Village Radio, the appearance that starts the road back.

years.h: Two nights at Webster Hall
years.p: Ferraro, Porcell, Siegler and Pincus, with [[Charlie Garriga|4f24f7e7-bc37-45d1-8f60-99bc992cd780]] on second guitar. Tours of the US, South America and Europe follow through 2014 and 2015.

years.h: There Will Be Quiet: The Story of Judge
years.p: A roughly hour-long documentary in four parts, directed by Seth Lowery and Siegler, premieres through the Village Voice and Noisey.

eras.title: Night one in Los Angeles
eras.text: Judge stayed a working reunion band, the heavy end of the Revelation family on its big bills, with Porcell and Siegler still behind Ferraro.

years.h: The Book of Revelation Records, Los Angeles
years.p: Judge co-headline night one at 1720 with 7 Seconds. Youth of Today and [[Side By Side|8dc812b1-d387-4c45-8173-f0d5bd0c318f]] take night two.

years.h: Home to the chickens
years.p: Between shows the singer of the angriest band on Revelation lives quietly: according to Wikipedia, Ferraro raises chickens on a family farm in West Virginia.
